title: The Circles and the Current: the Founder of the Bund, from Vilna to Toulouse and Back
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Sventsian, Vilna, and the Technical Track

stops.name: Sventsian, born in the Vilna Governorate
stops.date_confidence: the day and month come from the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon entry, which also supplies the detail about the father; encyclopedia.com gives only the year and the town. Coordinates corrected to the town centre of Svencionys, the pool's 55.1394, 26.1719 having sat about 1.4 km east-north-east of it.
stops.campa: Aron Iosifovich Kremer is born in Sventsian, a district town of Vilna Governorate inside the Pale of Settlement, into a household that keeps the law and reads the Haskalah. His father teaches Hebrew and is remembered as an enlightened man, which in this province and this decade means a man who wants his son taught arithmetic as well as Talmud. Everyone who follows him will call him Arkadi. The town is small, wooden, and Jewish in its majority, and the governorate around it holds the densest concentration of Jewish artisans in Europe.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Svencionys, Vilna Governorate, in the 1860s
sources: YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe, 'Kremer, Arkadii'

stops.name: Vilna, the Realschule
stops.date_confidence: circa. The Congress for Jewish Culture entry says he moved to Vilna at about twelve and entered a Realschule; no school register was located, and the month and day are defaulted to open the year.
stops.campa: At about twelve he is sent from the district town to Vilna and enters a Realschule, the modern secondary track: mathematics, drawing, physics, no Greek. It is neither the classical gymnasium nor the yeshiva. In that schoolroom he learns the two subjects he will spend fifty years teaching other people, how numbers behave and how machines do. Vilna at this moment holds the Romm printing house, the courtyard of the Gaon's synagogue, and a Jewish working class of tailors, tanners and bristle-workers that nobody has yet tried to organize.
suggested_refs: The Vilna Realschule and the modern technical secondary track in the Russian Empire

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the Technological Institute
stops.date_confidence: the decade is attested, the year is not. Sources place him at the Saint Petersburg Technological Institute in the 1880s with no matriculation date; 1885 is a mid-decade placement to order the segment and asserts nothing. Coordinates corrected to the Institute's own campus on Moskovsky Prospekt.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Technological Institute on Moskovsky Prospekt, among the empire's engineers in training, and finds there the other thing the capital keeps: student circles, forbidden pamphlets, and contact with Proletariat, the Polish Marxist organization. He studies steam and electricity by day and the Russian question at night. The technical education stops where the police work starts, and twenty-five years will pass before he is permitted to finish it, in another country, at forty-nine. He leaves without a degree.
suggested_refs: The Saint Petersburg Technological Institute and its student circles in the 1880s
The Polish Marxist party Proletariat, founded 1882
sources: H. Shukman, 'The Relations between the Jewish Bund and the RSDRP, 1897-1903' (Oxford D.Phil. thesis, 1961)

stops.name: Riga, the Polytechnic
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Riga Polytechnic appears only in the lexicon tradition relayed by the Congress for Jewish Culture entry; no register, faculty, or enrolment date was found in any source reachable this pass, and the date is a placement inside the 1880s, not a claim.
stops.campa: Biographical tradition also puts him at the Riga Polytechnic in these years, one more of the technical schools the empire built and then filled with the young men who would try to bring it down. Riga is a Baltic port, German in its faculty, imperial in its charter, full of Jewish and Latvian students who move between engineering and politics without drawing a line. Whether he matriculated there, and for how long, no register anyone can now reach will say.
suggested_refs: The Riga Polytechnic Institute and its Russian-imperial student body in the 1880s

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the first arrest
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month and day are not recorded and are defaulted. Encyclopedia.com and the Congress for Jewish Culture entry both carry the arrest; neither names the charge, the prison, or the length of the sentence.
stops.campa: He is arrested for revolutionary activity, held, and then barred from residing in the capital. It is the standard imperial sentence: remove the man from the city where he is dangerous and return him to the province where nobody yet knows him. What the sentence accomplishes is the reverse of its intention, since it puts a trained engineer with Petersburg politics back into a Jewish working town of a hundred thousand people who have never been organized. The charge, the prison and the term are in no file that can now be opened.
suggested_refs: Administrative exile and residence bans as the ordinary Russian sentence for student politics

stops.name: Vilna, the return and the group with no name
stops.date_confidence: the two lenses of the research disagree: the chronology gives 1889 for the arrival with Pati, the geography lens gives 1890 for the return after release, and Wikipedia has him released in 1890 after the 1889 arrest and exile. 1890 is used and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes back to Vilna, and Matilda Srednitskaia, called Pati, comes from Petersburg too. They marry, and they will work as a single organization for forty-five years. What they have is a method taken from the Russian populists and turned on a new object, the Yiddish-speaking workshop: teach the workers, in their own language, until they can teach each other. The group has no name, no press, no money and no legal existence. Around them a handful gather: Timofei Kopelzon, Shmuel Gozhanskii, John Mill, Isai Aiznshtat.
suggested_refs: The Vilna Jewish Social Democratic Group, 1890-1897
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.3

stops.name: Vilna, teaching the workers' circles
stops.date_confidence: 1891 is attested as the year from which encyclopedia.com dates his central organizing role; the circle numbers come from Shukman citing the Kopelzon and Evzorov memoirs and are memoir figures, not a count. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The method is called propaganda and it is done in rooms. Five or ten artisans at a time, a paraffin lamp, and Kremer at the table teaching political economy, history and mathematics. He teaches arithmetic to people who cannot do arithmetic, because arithmetic is the door into everything else on the syllabus. By the early nineties the intelligentsia circles number sixty or seventy and the workers' circles hold at least a hundred and fifty men. He is the acknowledged head of it. The whole apparatus fits inside a few apartments.
stops.quote: central organizer in the Jewish Social Democratic Group in Vilna from 1891-1897
suggested_refs: The Vilna workers' circles and the propaganda method, c. 1890-1894
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.3
eleven.co.il, Russian Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Kremer' (URL now returning 404)

stops.name: Vilna, Martov joins the circle
stops.date_confidence: 1893 attested in Shukman for Martov's arrival in Vilna under exile from Saint Petersburg; month and day not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Julius Martov, exiled from Petersburg as Kremer had been, arrives in Vilna and joins the circle. He is twenty, and he will end as the leader of Menshevism; here he is a young man learning Yiddish agitation from people who have been doing it for three years. The Vilna group at this moment is the most advanced socialist organization in the empire and almost nobody outside the Pale knows it exists. The question it is arguing with itself is the question that will define Russian Marxism: teach a hundred men well, or reach ten thousand badly.
suggested_refs: Julius Martov's Vilna exile, 1893-1895, and his Yiddish agitational work
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.3

stops.name: Vilna, writing On Agitation
stops.date_confidence: the sources split between 1893 and 1894 for the drafting: Wikipedia dates the pamphlet 1893 and credits it to Kremer with Martov, the Russian Jewish Encyclopedia and Shukman give 1894. 1894 is used and the range is flagged. It circulated in manuscript for two years before the 1896 Geneva printing.
stops.campa: Kremer writes Ob agitatsii and Martov edits it. The argument is short, and it travels in handwritten copies for two years, changing the practice of Russian Social Democracy before a press ever touches it. The circles produce excellent socialists at a rate of a dozen a year; the strike produces them by the hundred. So go into the workshop, take up the grievance the workers already have, the hours, the fines, the wage, and let the strike teach what the reading circle cannot.
stops.quote: from closed circles of socialist propaganda to action among the masses adapted to their actual economic requirements
stops.quote_source: encyclopedia.com, 'Kremer, Arkadi', on the effect of Ob agitatsii
suggested_refs: Ob agitatsii (On Agitation), drafted in Vilna, circulated in manuscript 1894-1896
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.20

stops.name: Geneva, before the Emancipation of Labour group
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the two lenses of the research contradict each other on the city: the chronology says Zurich, the geography lens says Geneva and flags the meeting as unconfirmed. Geneva is used because the Emancipation of Labour group was based there. No source reached this pass confirms that the meeting happened at all.
stops.campa: Tradition sends him to Switzerland to see the founders: Georgii Plekhanov, Pavel Axelrod, Vera Zasulich, the Emancipation of Labour group, who are the Russian Marxist movement abroad and who have almost no organization behind them at home. He asks them to represent the Russian Social Democrats to the International. Plekhanov answers that he cannot represent a movement which is not one movement. If the story is true, that refusal is what sends Kremer home to build the thing whose absence he has just been told about. Whether the meeting happened at all, no source reached will say.
suggested_refs: The Emancipation of Labour group at Geneva: Plekhanov, Axelrod, Zasulich
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, pp.22, 29
Geneva coordinate inherited from vladimir_medem.journey.json, the corpus pin for Bund and Russian emigre Geneva

stops.name: Geneva, On Agitation goes to press
stops.date_confidence: year attested through the GARF archival catalogue record for the pamphlet, fond 1741, opis 2, delo 624, cited via docs.historyrussia.org; the month is not recorded and is defaulted.
stops.campa: The Union of Russian Social Democrats Abroad prints Ob agitatsii in Geneva, with a postscript supplied by Axelrod. A pamphlet copied by hand in Vilna kitchens for two years becomes an object with a print run, and it travels: into Petersburg, into Moscow, into the strike waves of the middle nineties. Eleven years later the Minister of Justice will still be quoting the text in an official report as the document that explains where the Russian labour movement turned. The author's name is not on it.
suggested_refs: Ob agitatsii, Geneva imprint of the Union of Russian Social Democrats Abroad, 1896, with Axelrod's postscript
sources: State Archive of the Russian Federation (GARF), fond 1741 op.2 delo 624, catalogue record via docs.historyrussia.org
H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.20, citing Muravev's 1907 report

stops.name: Kyiv, the conference Vilna does not attend
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Shukman, citing Eidelman, carries the March 1897 Kyiv conference; the Jewish Virtual Library account of the pre-founding unification talks does not mention Kyiv, and the meeting could not be confirmed from any source fetched this pass. The day is defaulted.
stops.campa: An attempt is made at Kyiv to gather the scattered social democratic organizations into a party. Vilna does not come. The distance between the Jewish organizations of the northwest, working in Yiddish among a hundred thousand artisans, and the Russian committees of the south, working in Russian among factory hands, is not yet crossed by anything but correspondence. Kremer draws the opposite conclusion from most of the delegates. The Jewish organizations must unify first, as one body, and then join.
suggested_refs: The pre-1898 unification talks among the Vilna, Kyiv and Petersburg social democratic groups
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, pp.29, 39, citing Eidelman

stops.name: Vilna, thirteen delegates in an upper room
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Jewish Virtual Library gives 7-9 October 1897, thirteen delegates, eight of them working men; Wikipedia's 'September 1897' is the same congress rendered in the Julian calendar, not a rival date. The name used here is the founding name, General Jewish Labour Bund in Russia and Poland; Lithuania was added to the title only in 1901.
stops.campa: Thirteen delegates, eight of them working men, meet in an upper room in Vilna and constitute the General Jewish Labour Bund in Russia and Poland. Kremer opens the congress with the argument he has been making for a year: the Jewish workers need one central organization of their own, in their own language, inside the coming Russian party rather than outside it. He is elected to the first three-man Central Committee with Vladimir Kossovsky and Avrom Mutnik. Six weeks earlier, a thousand miles west at Basel, Theodor Herzl had opened a congress with the opposite answer to the same question.
stops.quote: a secret convention held in Vilna on Oct. 7-9, 1897, with the participation of 13 delegates (eight of them working men)
suggested_refs: The founding congress of the General Jewish Labour Bund, Vilna, 7-9 October 1897
The First Zionist Congress at Basel, 29-31 August 1897, the rival answer of the same season
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, pp.24, 27, citing John Mill, 'Arkadi un der ershter tsuzamenfor'
English Wikipedia, 'General Jewish Labour Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia'

stops.name: Minsk, the Central Committee moves
stops.date_confidence: Shukman places the Central Committee's move to Minsk after the founding congress, for security; no month is recorded and November is a placement inside 'late 1897'. The location of the press is not established by any source reached.
stops.campa: The Central Committee moves to Minsk, which is safer than Vilna for the single reason that Vilna is where the police have been looking. Kremer runs it. Within a few months it will be the best organized socialist body in the Russian Empire and the only one able to put a working delegation on a train to a founding congress. The Bund in its first year is three men, an illegal press, a courier network, and an organization of tailors and bristle-workers across the Pale who now have a name for the thing they belong to.
suggested_refs: The Bund's Central Committee and illegal press at Minsk, 1897-1898
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.27

stops.name: Minsk, the First Congress of the RSDLP
stops.date_confidence: March 1898 attested; the exact days and the meeting house are not established in the sources reached. Shukman gives the Central Committee election, the Jewish Virtual Library gives the delegate arithmetic.
stops.campa: Nine delegates meet in Minsk in March and found the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. Three of the nine are Bundists. The Bund brings the press, the couriers and the only functioning mass organization in the empire, and it is admitted with autonomy in matters concerning the Jewish proletariat specifically. For about four months he is one of three men formally at the head of Russian Marxism. Kremer is elected to the new party's three-man Central Committee with Boris Eidelman and Stepan Radchenko. He is thirty-two.
stops.quote: three of the nine delegates were Bundists
suggested_refs: The First Congress of the RSDLP, Minsk, March 1898, and the Bund's autonomy clause
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, pp.1, 45

stops.name: Minsk, the whole leadership taken in a day
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date, the four months of surveillance and the arrest totals come from Shukman citing Menshchikov's 'Okhrana i revoliutsiia' and were not independently confirmed this pass. 26 July is presumably Old Style, as Russian police records of the period are, but no source consulted says so.
stops.campa: Sergei Zubatov's Moscow secret police have been watching for four months. On the twenty-sixth of July they take all three members of the Bund's Central Committee at once, seize the presses at Bobruisk and at Minsk, and arrest between fifty-five and seventy people. The Bund survives the decapitation, which is the first proof that it is an organization and not a circle. The party founded in March has its leadership removed in July, and of the nine men who met in Minsk almost none are at liberty by the end of the year.
suggested_refs: Zubatov's Moscow Okhrana operation against the Bund, July 1898
The seized Bund presses at Bobruisk and Minsk
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.38, citing Menshchikov, 'Okhrana i revoliutsiia'

stops.name: Moscow, the prison and the coding machine
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on two counts. No source reached places the imprisonment in Moscow or gives its length: encyclopedia.com says only that he escaped abroad in 1900 following imprisonment, naming no city, and the Moscow location and the two-year term rest on Shukman alone. The coordinates are the generic Moscow centre. The cipher machine is Wikipedia's, sourced to the same 1961 thesis.
stops.campa: He is held, by the tradition, in Moscow, for close to two years. What he did there is the most repeated story about him and the least documented: that he turned his mathematics on the problem of secrecy and produced a cipher system and a coding machine which the revolutionary movement afterwards used. That he worked in codes is certain, and Lenin's letter to him proves that much four years later. The claim travels through one doctoral thesis of 1961, and beneath it no patent, no description and no party record has been found.
stops.quote: put his technological and mathematical studies to use by developing a system of cryptography and a coding machine that came to be widely used in the Russian revolutionary movement
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Arkadi Kremer', citing H. Shukman's 1961 thesis
suggested_refs: H. Shukman, 'The Relations between the Jewish Bund and the RSDRP, 1897-1903' (Oxford D.Phil. thesis, 1961), the sole authority for the cipher claim

segments.name: The Foreign Committee: Geneva, London, Paris

stops.name: Geneva, the Foreign Committee
stops.date_confidence: 1900 attested for the departure from Russia, though encyclopedia.com words it as an escape rather than a release and no source describes a release. The month is not recorded. The Chemin des Pervenches address and the proofreader listing come from Swiss administrative material not reachable this pass and are unverified.
stops.campa: In 1900 he leaves Russia, by the one reachable account an escape rather than a release, and takes up the Bund's Foreign Committee in Geneva: the money, the printing, the correspondence with the International, the routes back over the border. Several hundred Russian revolutionaries occupy a few streets of this city, all publishing at one another, and the Bund's committee is among the better funded, because Jewish workers abroad send money home. Swiss records of the emigration are said to list him as a proofreader living on the Chemin des Pervenches.
stops.quote: Following imprisonment for revolutionary activities, he escaped abroad in 1900
suggested_refs: The Bund's Foreign Committee at Geneva and its clandestine press, 1900-1901

stops.name: Geneva, expelled by the Federal Council
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date, the co-defendant Chaim Bernstein and the petition of more than a hundred supporters come from academic literature summarising a Swiss Federal Archives expulsion protocol; the protocol itself could not be fetched, and no page retrieved this pass confirms the event directly.
stops.campa: After an anti-Russian demonstration the Swiss authorities detain Kremer and Chaim Bernstein. A lawyer appears for them and more than a hundred people petition on their behalf, and the Federal Council expels them from the country anyway. The neutral republic that shelters the whole Russian emigration shelters it for exactly as long as it stays quiet. He has been out of prison a year. He packs the committee's papers and its correspondence, which is what a headquarters actually consists of, and goes.
suggested_refs: The Swiss Federal Council expulsion protocol of 17 April 1901 concerning Kremer and Bernstein
sources: Swiss Federal Archives / Geneva State Archives expulsion protocol, summarised in 'East European Jews in Switzerland' (dokumen.pub); the primary record was not reachable

stops.name: London, the Foreign Committee in the East End
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. No source fetched this pass documents the route through Paris, the London relocation, or the transfer of the committee's press in 1901; the sequence is inferred from where the committee is before and after. The month is a placement in late summer, not a record.
stops.campa: Through Paris he takes the Foreign Committee to London, to the Jewish East End: Whitechapel, the sweatshops, Yiddish signboards, socialist and anarchist papers arguing with each other in a language the English around them cannot read. The Bund's press and its foreign correspondence set up among immigrant tailors who left the same towns his organizers are working in. Der Veker is printed in this milieu. None of this move is documented in anything that can now be fetched, and the year itself is a reconstruction.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish socialist press of the London East End around 1901, including Der Veker
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, on Foreign Committee operations
YIVO and Congress for Jewish Culture biographical tradition; no primary confirmation located

stops.name: Bialystok, five delegates get away
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens tags this attested through Shukman, citing Iskra no. 26 and Kremer's own manuscript notes in the Bund Archives; the geography lens could not confirm it independently. March 1902 is used with the day defaulted, and the conflict between the two lenses is left standing.
stops.campa: He crosses the frontier illegally to represent the Bund at a social democratic conference in Bialystok, a textile town with a large Jewish working class where the practical questions can be settled among the people who will have to carry them out. Within a week the police liquidate the organizing body the conference had set up. Five delegates escape arrest and Kremer is one of the five. He writes his own account of the conference afterwards, one of the few pages in his own hand about his own work. The manuscript is in the Bund Archives, unpublished and undigitized.
suggested_refs: 'Zametki A. Kremera o belostokskoi konferentsii', Bund Archives manuscript
Iskra no. 26 on the Bialystok conference and its liquidation
sources: H. Shukman, Oxford D.Phil. thesis 1961, p.100

stops.name: Paris, the letter about invisible ink
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated 4 May 1902 and was read in full at marxists.org, printed from Leninskii Sbornik XIII. Lenin wrote from London; that Kremer was in Paris and was the 'Alexander' addressed comes from the editorial apparatus rather than from the letter's own text.
stops.campa: Lenin writes from London to Paris, to a man he knows as Alexander. The Iskra delegate Fedor Dan is thought to have been arrested and the contacts he carried are lost with him: who else sits on the organizing committee, and how does one reach them. Nine years of clandestine practice are treated in the letter as routine, one professional to another, fifteen months before the two of them stop being on the same side. What it proposes is invisible ink, a key handed to the bearer in person, a courier trusted to decide by himself if something urgent happens.
stops.quote: We have good reason to fear that our delegate (to the conference) was arrested soon after the conference, before he had time to hand over his office. We therefore ask you to let us know: 1) who besides our delegate was elected to the preparatory (or organising, etc.) committee? and 2) how can we contact these people (address, key, password, etc.)? You might write your communication in invisible ink in code, if necessary, giving the key to the bearer of this letter personally.
stops.quote_source: V. I. Lenin, Letter to A. I. Kremer, 4 May 1902, Collected Works, from Leninskii Sbornik XIII, read at marxists.org
suggested_refs: V. I. Lenin, 'Letter to A. I. Kremer', 4 May 1902
The Paris coordinate carried in vladimir_lenin.journey.json as the corpus pin

segments.name: The Congress That Split, and the Return

stops.name: Brussels, the Second Congress opens
stops.date_confidence: the congress opened in Brussels in late July 1903 and transferred to London under police pressure. The marxists.org delegate list confirms the pseudonym Wolf as A. I. Kremer, 1865-1935. The precise opening day is given variously in the literature and is used here only to order the stop.
stops.campa: The Second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party opens in Brussels, and the Belgian police take an interest almost at once. Kremer sits with the Bund delegation under the party name Wolf, with a consultative vote. The Bund comes into the room with the largest organization any delegation has, and with the demand he has carried since the upper room in Vilna six years before: recognition as the sole representative of the Jewish proletariat, inside a party built on federal lines. Under police pressure the congress will finish in London.
suggested_refs: The delegate list of the Second Congress of the RSDLP, 1903, and its pseudonyms
sources: marxists.org, RSDLP 1903 Second Congress delegate biographies

stops.name: London, the Bund walks out
stops.date_confidence: August 1903 attested for the London sessions, the rejection of the Bund's federal demand and the walkout; the day is defaulted, different sources dating the individual sessions differently. The London coordinate is the corpus pin used in vladimir_lenin.journey.json and leon_trotsky.journey.json.
stops.campa: The congress reconvenes in London and votes the demand down. Lenin and Martov, who are not yet at opposite ends of anything, stand together on this one and carry the majority with them. Days later that majority and that minority will split from each other over something else. The Bund delegation withdraws and leaves the party it helped found five years earlier. Walking out beside Kremer is Vladimir Medem, newly co-opted to the Foreign Committee, who will spend twenty years writing the theory of national cultural autonomy this vote declined to hear.
suggested_refs: The 1903 minutes of the Second Congress of the RSDLP and the Bund's secession
sources: marxists.org, RSDLP 1903 Second Congress delegate biographies

stops.name: New York, the money that comes back east
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The visit is carried by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon tradition; no itinerary, city or date was located in any reachable source, and New York is inferred from Abraham Cahan's base at the Forward. The month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic, the only time in his life he leaves Europe, and the American Bundist network he finds and cultivates will keep money moving east for a generation. Abraham Cahan of the Forward, who came out of the same northwestern milieu, remembers the visit afterwards in a sketch he titles Kremer in amerike. What survives of the whole episode is the fact of the crossing and the network that came out of it. The dates, the cities and the route are in no source that can be reached.
suggested_refs: Abraham Cahan, 'Kremer in amerike', recollection of the 1904 visit

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, back for the revolution
stops.date_confidence: the 1905 return to Russia is attested in encyclopedia.com. The association with the Petersburg Soviet is not in that source or any other reached this pass and is carried here as tradition only. The month is not recorded.
stops.campa: The revolution opens Russia and he goes back into it. Strikes run from Baku to Warsaw, the Bund puts tens of thousands of members and its armed self-defence groups into the streets, and for a few months in the autumn the empire is negotiating with its own workers. Later biographers place him around the Petersburg Soviet, though no source that can be checked says so. The return itself is certain, into the country that had jailed him twice and barred him from this city. He is forty years old.
stops.quote: he returned to Russia in 1905 to continue Bund work
suggested_refs: The Bund in the 1905 Revolution and its self-defence groups
sources: eleven.co.il, Russian Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Kremer' (URL now returning 404)

stops.name: Russia, the second arrest
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on every particular. The 1907 arrest comes from the lexicon tradition alone; the charge, the place of detention, the sentence and the release date are unestablished, the place is unspecified in the sources, and the coordinate is the Saint Petersburg pin used for want of any location at all.
stops.campa: The reaction closes the opening. Stolypin's field courts hang men by the thousand, the parties are driven back underground, and Kremer is arrested again. The charge, the prison, the sentence and the date of release are in no record that can now be reached, and the arrest itself rests on the biographical tradition. He is forty-two and has been a revolutionary for twenty years. Within three years the Bund's membership will have fallen from tens of thousands to a few thousand.
suggested_refs: The Stolypin reaction and the collapse of Bund membership, 1907-1910

stops.name: Russia, leaving the underground
stops.date_confidence: encyclopedia.com's timeline gives 1908 for the abandonment of political life; the lexicon tradition has him remaining a member or associate of the Bund. The month is not recorded, the place is unspecified, and the coordinate is again the Saint Petersburg pin used for want of a location.
stops.campa: He comes out and stops. It is not a break with the Bund, which he never leaves, and it is not a recantation. It is a withdrawal from full-time underground work by a man who has decided he is no longer the most useful person in it. He is forty-three, with no profession and no completed degree. The founder of the largest Jewish socialist organization in the world spends the next four years as a private individual, and the record for those years is empty.
suggested_refs: The Bund in the years of reaction, 1908-1912

stops.name: Toulouse, enrolled at forty-seven
stops.date_confidence: 1912 attested for the settlement in France and the enrolment at the Toulouse Electrotechnical Institute; the month is not recorded and is defaulted.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Electrotechnical Institute in Toulouse, in the French southwest, to finish at forty-seven the education the Petersburg police interrupted at twenty-four. Twenty-three years lie in the gap, and inside them a party, two congresses, two arrests, a prison, an expulsion and a revolution. Nobody in the lecture hall knows what he founded. He sits examinations beside students young enough to be his children, in a language not his own, in a discipline that has been remade since he last studied it.
suggested_refs: The Institut electrotechnique de Toulouse and its prewar cohort

stops.name: Toulouse, the engineer's diploma
stops.date_confidence: 1914 attested for the graduation through the Congress for Jewish Culture entry; no month is recorded, and the defaulted date should not be read as placing the diploma before the outbreak of war in August.
stops.campa: He graduates as an engineer. From this year to the end of his life he will be paid for knowing how current behaves in a wire, and the whole second half of his working life takes place inside that trade. The revolutionary of the nineties becomes the thing the Technological Institute set out to make of him in the first place, thirty years late and in a foreign country. The diploma is issued in the year the continent goes to war, and he will spend that war at a drawing board in the French southwest. He is forty-nine.
stops.quote: graduating in 1914 from the Toulouse Electrotechnical Institute as an engineer
suggested_refs: The 1914 engineering diploma of the Toulouse Electrotechnical Institute

stops.name: France, the war years without a word
stops.date_confidence: encyclopedia.com's timeline covers 1912-1921 as years of engineering work in France without specifying a place; the Entente alignment comes from biographical tradition and is unverified by any text of his own. The 1916 date is a midpoint placement, and the coordinate is the Toulouse pin for want of a recorded workplace.
stops.campa: He works as an electrical engineer in France through the war. The Second International has broken apart over it, each party voting its own government's war credits, and the biographical tradition puts him with the socialists who backed the Entente. The man who wrote the pamphlet that turned Russian Marxism leaves no surviving sentence in his own hand about the largest political event of his lifetime. No text by him about the war has been found: no article, no letter, no speech, no minute.

stops.name: Vilna, the return after twenty years
stops.date_confidence: 1921 attested for the return of both Arkadi and Pati Kremer to Vilna, from encyclopedia.com and the Congress for Jewish Culture entry on Pati; the month is not recorded.
stops.campa: Arkadi and Pati Kremer come back to Vilna after twenty years abroad. The city is Wilno now, in the Second Polish Republic, taken from Lithuania the year before. The empire they conspired against has gone, and so has the party that outvoted them in London, which rules Russia and is in the process of closing the Bund down inside it. He is fifty-six. He takes work teaching mathematics and electrical engineering; Pati goes back into the Vilna organization, where she will stay for the rest of her life.

stops.campa: He teaches first-year electrical engineering at the Vilna Technicum, the ORT vocational school, and at the Teacher Seminar besides. The founder of the Bund is a man with a timetable now, showing sixteen-year-olds how a motor turns. A student course record survives from this year, Leon Daniel's, signed by the director Israel Okun: a year of work set out term by term in a school that trains Jewish workers' children for trades, in a language the Polish state does not examine in.

stops.name: Vilna, Elektrotekhnik, Part I
stops.date_confidence: 1927 attested for Part I through the Center for Jewish History blog post; the Congress for Jewish Culture entry dates his technical publishing in Vilna more broadly to 1925-1936. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: There is no textbook of electrical engineering in Yiddish, so he writes one. Elektrotekhnik, Part I, covers the first five terms of the Technicum course, handwritten and then lithographed, because a typeset technical book in Yiddish would cost more than the school or its students could pay. It is the arithmetic lessons of the Vilna kitchens of 1891 again, done with different material. Every term, every formula, every part of a machine has to be given a Yiddish name, some of them for the first time in the language.

stops.name: Vilna, Part II and the cover by Shkop
stops.date_confidence: corrected against the pool: the Center for Jewish History blog describes the second edition of Part II as a 1928-1929 issue, not a 1928 one. The date shown opens the span. The issuing body, the mutual-aid administration of the Technicum, and the cover illustration by Yitskhok Shkop are confirmed in the blog.
stops.campa: The mutual-aid administration of the Technicum issues Part II in a second edition, lithographed again, distributed at a price the students can actually meet, with a cover drawn by Yitskhok Shkop. A school with no money produces its own textbooks and its own cover art. The pages carry what a first-year course needs: circuits, windings, the symbols for resistance and current, all of it captioned in the language the students speak at home. Kremer is sixty-three, and the volumes are in his own handwriting.

The lexicon tradition makes him chairman of the Vilna organization and the Bund's man on the Jewish Community Council. Interwar Polish Bundism runs on younger people, and what he supplies is that the founder is alive and still in the room. The sources that can be opened say only that he resumed activity and became a moral authority, which is a different sort of position and is probably the truer description.

stops.name: Vilna, the photograph with the grandson
stops.date_confidence: the photograph is dated 1930 in the Center for Jewish History record reproduced on Wikimedia Commons, and its caption names no one but Kremer and an unnamed grandson. The identification of the child as Joseph Dobrinsky is an inference and is not in the source. The place is not stated in the caption either; Vilna is where he was living.
stops.campa: A photograph is taken: an old man in a dark suit holding an infant, both of them looking into the camera. It is the clearest surviving image of the domestic half of a life otherwise spent in rooms that could be raided at any hour. The caption the archive kept says only Arkadi Kremer and his grandson. The child is most likely a son of his daughter Vera, who had married the painter Isaac Dobrinsky in Paris in 1926, but no source names him, and the archive did not record where the picture was made.

stops.name: Vilna, death at seventy
stops.date_confidence: 20 September 1935 attested, the Congress for Jewish Culture entry and the marxists.org congress delegate biography agreeing on the death; encyclopedia.com gives the year. No cause of death is documented in any source consulted.
stops.campa: He dies in Vilna on the twentieth of September, seventy years old. He had outlived the empire he fought; the party he founded had been suppressed in Russia by the men who outvoted him in London, and in Poland it was the largest Jewish workers' organization in the country. He had spent his last thirteen years teaching electrical engineering to the children and grandchildren of the tailors he organized as a young man, and some of those pupils were still in the Technicum that autumn. No cause of death is recorded anywhere reachable.

stops.name: Uzupis, the cemetery across the river
stops.date_confidence: inference, not record. No burial register entry and no gravestone for Kremer has been located; the Uzupis cemetery is identified only because it was the Jewish burial ground of Vilna in this period. Coordinates corrected: the pool's 54.6935, 25.265 pointed north-west toward the older Snipiskes ground, which had closed in 1831 and cannot be the site.
stops.campa: He is almost certainly buried in the Uzupis Jewish cemetery across the Vilnia river, the ground Vilna's Jews had used since 1831. No register entry has been found for him and no gravestone has been located, and the position of the grave inside the ground is unknown. The cemetery was demolished under Soviet rule in the 1960s and its stones carried off for building work, some of them laid as steps in the city. A memorial stands at the former entrance now.

Vilna, where he had lived and taught and been buried seven years earlier, is under German occupation while the volume is being set. stops.name: Vilna, Pati by eight years
stops.date_confidence: September 1943 attested for the liquidation of the Vilna ghetto; the Congress for Jewish Culture entry on Pati Srednitski gives 1943 for her death and the sources it summarises disagree on the killing site, naming either Sobibor or Ponary. stops.campa: Pati Kremer, born in Vilna on 2 January 1867, who came from Petersburg in 1890 to build the circles with him and stayed in the movement for fifty years, is killed in the liquidation of the Vilna ghetto. The sources disagree about where: Sobibor, or the pits at Ponary in the woods outside the city. She had gone on working in the Vilna Bund for eight years after his death. Of the two people who began the organization, one lies in an unmarked grave and the other in a place that cannot be named.

stops.name: Minneapolis, the Bund on a bestseller list
stops.date_confidence: 2026 attested as the publication year through the publisher's own page; the month is not recorded and is defaulted. The bestseller placing and the fourth printing within three days are the publisher's claims, reported as such. The coordinate is Milkweed Editions in Minneapolis, not a place Kremer ever went.
stops.campa: A narrative history of the Bund is published in Minneapolis, with Pati and Arkadi Kremer at its centre. It enters the New York Times list at number four and goes into a fourth printing inside three days. The organization thirteen people constituted in an upper room in Vilna, suppressed in Russia, destroyed in Poland and outlived by its exiles, is being read now by people who have never encountered the word doikayt. What they are reading about is a tailors' movement with a theory about where home is.
